REV64: The revision study compared the gate with simpler alternatives (Fig. 6a; Supplementary Table S4). On its two seeds, ungated CA-LS saved 8.31% and 9.7% of its runs were traps; with the gate it saved 6.92% [5.53, 8.52] and 3.7% [2.0, 5.7] were traps. No alternative dominated the gate, in the sense fixed in the plan: none had both a higher saving and fewer traps with paired intervals that exclude zero. The α sweep traces a smooth trade-off. At α = 0.5 the gate behaves like no gate, because the median difference error is close to zero, and α = 0.95 halves the traps again for 0.86 points of saving. A single threshold for all lags and horizons gave up 0.79 points [0.42, 1.20] of saving at the same trap rate, so binning by lag and horizon pays for itself. The level-interval rule almost removed traps (0.6%) but kept only 58% of the ungated saving, the cost of the large threshold seen in Fig. 3c. Capping deferrals at 6 h without a gain threshold left 7.6% of runs as traps. Because it defers fewer tasks, the gate also halved deadline misses on GB (23.4% against 44.0%; Section 6.5), and on the heterogeneous platform at f ≥ 2.0 but not at f = 1.2. A planner that uses the uncertainty of the forecast directly fared no better (exploratory). CA-LS planning on the upper 0.9-quantile of the forecast for each horizon, the same bound the level-interval rule uses, saved 7.97% with 9.1% traps. It barely differed from planning on the point forecast, because a horizon-dependent bias moves the costs of nearby windows together. Filtering individual deferrals by their difference error, as the gate does, is what reduced traps. Controlling the risk of the whole plan did not do better either (exploratory; development data, two pilots with 20 and 40 submissions, each with a decision rule fixed in advance). A planner that minimises the mean emissions over error trajectories of past vintages, subject to a cap on the share of these scenarios in which the plan is a trap, and certifies the plan on held-out scenarios, kept the realised trap rate below its target in every setting (0.0–6.0% for targets of 5–20%). Its saving–risk points lay close to the gate's (Fig. 6b): a version that selects among candidate plans lay slightly above it (for example, 8.88% saving with 4.1% traps against 8.35% with 4.6% for the gate at α = 0.9), and a version that optimises over the scenarios lay on or below it (9.15% with 6.0% traps against 9.45% with 7.0% at α = 0.8). The differences were within the statistical uncertainty, and both pilots failed their usefulness criterion. Once the forecast at submission is fixed, the remaining choice is how much risk to accept, and a simple gate exposes that choice as well as a scenario-based optimiser.
REV65: Carbon-aware plans missed deadlines far more often than HEFT when task runtimes varied. In the main study, with issued forecasts and the static executor, CA-LS missed 31–49% of deadlines across f, against 0–1.5% for HEFT; CaWoSched and Shift missed 15–46%, and the gate roughly halved the rates (14–25%). On GB this was a secondary outcome; the sealed tests on the other grids (E4a) and the heterogeneous platform (G5) found the same pattern (Table 5). Most misses were small overruns: for CA-LS the median tardiness of a missed run was 1.5% of the deadline, the 90th percentile 5.2% and the 99th percentile 12.5%. A missed deadline is nevertheless a failure for the user. Runtime noise also reduced the realised saving slightly, from 8.31% to 7.74% for CA-LS with the static executor (revision study).
REV65B: Fig. 7 shows the two remedies tested in the revision study. The reactive executor, which starts delayed work as soon as it is ready, reduced the gap between CA-LS and HEFT from 36–48 to 22–35 percentage points; every lower bound stayed above 17 points, so by the sealed reading the result is robust to the executor (Q2). Once an ancestor has overrun, deferred work already sits close to the deadline, and starting it early no longer helps. A slack reserve was far more effective (Q3). Planning against D′ = M + 0.75(D − M) cut misses from 44.0% to 3.6% (2.8% with the reactive executor) while keeping 81% of the saving (6.76% against 8.31%). The remaining gap to HEFT was 10 points at f = 1.2, 3 at f = 1.5 and none at f ≥ 2.0. With ρ = 0.5 misses fell below 1% at 59% of the saving. The reserve did not change the share of the oracle saving kept under forecasts (R = 0.73 for both reserves against 0.72 without) and reduced traps only slightly (8.9% and 7.3% against 9.7%). Reserve and gate therefore address different risks and can be combined. Shift with the gate was the most conservative option (9.5% misses, 0.9% traps, 5.3% saving). The conclusions do not depend on independent task noise (exploratory). With a job-wide runtime factor added (same marginal spread), CA-LS missed 28–43% of deadlines, 28–38 points more than HEFT, and the reserve of 25% brought misses down to 6.9%, against 2.8% for HEFT.
DISC_RESERVE: Planning against a deadline that keeps a quarter of the slack in reserve cut misses from 44% to under 4% while keeping about four-fifths of the saving, and a work-conserving executor was no substitute for it [E].
Q6_TEXT: With the authors' own budget band (frac = 0.2 and 0.4; revision study, seeds 10–11) the picture was unchanged. CaWoSched with the safeguard saved 9.4–9.5% under the oracle and 7.2–7.3% under issued forecasts (R = 0.76–0.77; traps 9.1–9.2%), slightly less than with frac = 1.0 on the same seeds (10.2% and 7.9%). Raw CWM emitted more than HEFT on average with every band (−7.1% to −0.2% under the oracle), and with the safeguard it saved 4.3–4.6%.
REV63: Re-planning every 2 h on the newest vintage (6.2 re-plans per run on average) raised the forecast-based saving of CA-LS from 10.3% to 12.3% at f ≥ 1.5, or from 72% to 86% [78%, 92%] of the static oracle saving, on the two revision seeds (Q1). It did not reduce traps: 10.8% [7.0, 14.8] of re-planned runs were traps, against 9.7% without re-planning. The sealed reading required both an upper bound of R of at least 0.9 and an upper bound of the trap rate below 2%, so re-planning does not remove the problem. With the gate, re-planning gave R = 0.73 with 4.4% traps, again a higher saving at a similar risk. For Shift, re-planning changed little (R = 0.80 against 0.78; traps 10.7% against 11.1%), because the offset is fixed once the workflow has started.
REV63B: Two exploratory runs, added after the sealed results were known, separate the sources of this gain. Re-planning with oracle intensity raised the oracle saving from 14.3% to 15.7%, so the loop also optimises better than a single pass of local search. Re-planning on the submission-time vintage at every step saved 11.9%, only 0.37 points [−0.09, 0.92] less than re-planning on newer vintages. Relative to its own oracle, re-planning kept 78% [71%, 83%] of the saving, against 72% for the static scheduler. Newer forecasts therefore added little, and traps were as frequent with stale as with fresh vintages (10.2% against 10.8%). A plausible reason is that a deferral can be undone only before the deferred task starts, while a newer vintage that reveals the mistake often arrives later. Most of the error comes from the forecast available at submission, and later corrections come too late to undo it.
ABSTRACT: Carbon-aware workflow schedulers defer tasks into periods of cleaner electricity, but they are usually evaluated with perfect knowledge of future carbon intensity. We replay deadline-constrained DAG workflows against the carbon-intensity forecasts that the Great Britain grid operator actually issued, in a sequence of pre-registered studies with list and local-search schedulers, whole-workflow shifting and the official code of CaWoSched and CWM. In the confirmatory study (3,000 jobs), issued forecasts kept 68% [62%, 74%] of the oracle saving; this verdict held under the sealed analysis but not under clustering by week. About one plan in seven with moderate slack emitted more than a carbon-agnostic HEFT schedule; we call these outcomes carbon traps. A sealed extension to four further grids with model forecasts found a similar pooled loss (66% kept), but the share kept ranged from 19% to 85% across grids, which was associated with the ratio of forecast error to short-term variability (exploratory). A gate calibrated on errors of forecast differences cut traps by 8–9 percentage points while keeping 84–87% of the saving. In robustness analyses, no simpler gate dominated it, and neither planning on an upper forecast quantile nor re-planning on newer forecasts reduced traps. With runtime variability, carbon-aware plans on GB missed 31–49% of deadlines, against at most 1.5% for HEFT. Reserving a quarter of the slack cut misses to under 4% while keeping 81% of the saving. Whole-workflow shifting matched task-level scheduling under forecasts. Evaluations of carbon-aware schedulers should use issued forecasts and report traps and deadline misses.
INTRO_RESULTS: The answers are sobering but constructive. Issued forecasts kept about two-thirds of the oracle saving on GB, and model forecasts kept a similar share pooled over four other grids, but from a fifth to most of it depending on the grid. About one plan in seven with moderate slack became a carbon trap. Across grids, the loss was associated with the forecast error relative to the short-term variation of intensity. Re-planning on newer forecasts improved optimisation but added little information and did not reduce traps. A gate on forecast-difference errors reduced traps on every grid and platform at a modest cost in saving. Simple whole-workflow shifting did as well as task-level scheduling under forecasts. With runtime variability, carbon-aware plans missed a third to a half of their deadlines. Reserving slack removed most of these misses; a work-conserving executor did not. On a heterogeneous platform the loss was smaller, because much of the saving came from energy-aware mapping, which needs no forecast; the part due to timing was lost even more.
CONCLUSION: Carbon-aware workflow scheduling has been evaluated almost entirely with perfect foresight. Replayed against forecasts that were actually issued, a carbon-aware DAG scheduler kept about two-thirds of its oracle saving on GB, and about one plan in seven with moderate slack emitted more than a carbon-agnostic schedule. The official CaWoSched code lost a similar share, and CWM's native objective did not track emissions under our budget mapping. Across four further grids the share kept ranged from a fifth to most of the saving. Neither re-planning on newer forecasts nor planning on an upper forecast quantile removed traps, but a gate calibrated on errors of forecast differences reduced them on every grid, at a modest cost in saving. Whole-workflow shifting did as well as task-level scheduling, and it is a baseline that every evaluation should include. Carbon-aware plans also spend the slack that protects deadlines, and reserving part of it restored most of that protection. Across grids, the value of a forecast for scheduling was associated with its error relative to the short-term variation of intensity more than with its relative accuracy, which suggests judging forecasters by how well they rank windows. The evidence has limits: issued vintages for one grid and season, model forecasts for the others, simulated execution, and WfCommons workflows on small clusters. A pre-registered winter replication on GB is planned. Future work should replay issued forecasts from more grids and seasons, consider marginal intensity and shared clusters, and design schedulers that reason about the errors of forecast differences rather than levels. All plans, code and results are public, so others can repeat the evaluation with their own schedulers and forecasts.
